description: We are Delta L. We’re building an interactive map that shows where Earth’s surface changed beyond the normal (floods, vegetation loss, ground deformation), using NISAR radar as our base and cross-checking each alert with other satellites. Simple to use, with accuracy measured for real. We’re looking for: data analysis and geoprocessing (Python), web development and maps, design and data visualization, storytelling. We speak Portuguese and English.
summary: NISAR Anomaly Watch turns NISAR radar files into stories anyone can read. NISAR's L-band radar sees through clouds, smoke and night every 12 days, but its products (GCOV, GUNW, SME2) are hard to open and harder to interpret. Our app starts with an interactive globe showing all 17,006 real NISAR frames, built from 205,781 files in NASA's catalog. Any frame can be clicked for a quick comparison with the nearest optical scene. Three highlight areas show real results: a wildfire in California, the farming frontier in the Cerrado, and soil moisture on the Tocantins River. The core is a full analysis of a 13 × 13 km square in the Pantanal (Paiaguás, Brazil). Across 27 passes, the radar shows the surface changing in September 2026: 41% of the area lost coherence between Sep 8 and Sep 20, confirmed by two other independent passes (24% and 25%). Rain data explain why: the first rains after a dry winter. The app shows what changed, when, and why. It works in English and Portuguese, on desktop and mobile.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

NISAR Anomaly Watch is a web app that makes changes on Earth's surface visible using NISAR radar data. It works in three levels:

1. Globe: an interactive globe with all 17,006 real NISAR frames (ascending and descending), coloured by how many passes each has. Search any place and fly there.

2. Quick comparison: click any frame to see its NISAR products and the nearest cloud-free optical scene (Sentinel-2/Landsat), with NDVI before and after, fetched live.

3. Stories: three highlight areas (Norte Fire in California, the MATOPIBA farming frontier in the Cerrado, and the Tocantins River) and one full analysis of a 13 × 13 km square in the Pantanal (Paiaguás, Brazil), presented as a 12-step guide.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline finds NISAR files through NASA's CMR, downloads GCOV (HH/HV backscatter), GUNW (interferometric coherence) and SME2 (soil moisture) from the ASF DAAC with Earthdata Login, crops them to the study area, and computes the metrics. In Paiaguás: a time-lapse of 27 passes next to optical and C-band (Sentinel-1) images; the share of the area that lost coherence in each 12-day pair (41% between Sep 8 and Sep 20 against ~4% in other months, confirmed by two independent passes: 24% and 25%); a per-pixel classification of change (stable, abrupt drop or rise, gradual change, flooding, permanent water) in hectares; a map of when each abrupt change happened; and the HV history at one point. NASA POWER rain and soil moisture explain the cause: the first rains after a dry winter (21 mm on Sep 13). We test alternative explanations (fire, flooding) and show the limits, such as one unreliable pass and a calm control period.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Radar is the only sensor that sees the Pantanal, the Amazon and fire smoke every 12 days, day or night. Our app gives scientists, land managers, educators and the public a way to read those changes without opening HDF5 files: what changed, where, when and why, with every number traceable to its source file. The same method can be applied to any of the 17,006 frames.

TOOLS

Python (numpy, scipy, rasterio, h5py, xarray, matplotlib, pyproj, pystac-client, planetary-computer, odc-stac, earthaccess); JavaScript with D3 (orthographic globe on canvas); HTML/CSS; GitHub Pages. Bilingual (EN/PT), mobile-friendly, open source (MIT).

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

We treat the surface as a "waltz": some changes are predictable (seasons, floods), others are not (fire, sudden drying). The intro tells that story before any chart appears. Every chart was simplified for non-experts: plain units (1 ha = 100 × 100 m), one colour per period, no jargon such as track numbers, and a glossary always one click away. We followed NASA Web Design System spacing and type guidance, and we use no NASA logos.
